candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the `logFileName` HTTP query parameter of the authenticated admin REST resource `/management/domain/view-log/details` (registered as Domain -> LogViewerResource -> "view-log" in CommandResourceMetaData.java line 267, with the `details/` sub-resource exposed by LogViewerResource.java lines 116-119). The value is used directly as path data; `../` segments are not rejected anywhere in StructuredLogViewerResource, LogFilter, LogFilterForInstance, LogViewHandlers, LogViewerContentSource, or LogFile. Other query parameters (startIndex, maximumNumberOfResults, instanceName) only influence pagination/instance selection, not the path construction.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Searched the logging module (LogFilter, LogFilterForInstance, LogFile, LogParserFactory, RawLogParser), the REST resources (StructuredLogViewerResource, LogViewerResource, LogNamesResource), and the admin console handlers (LogViewHandlers, LogViewerContentSource, LogFilesContentSource) for any normalization, canonical-path containment, whitelist, or regex validation of `logFileName`; none exists in this snapshot. The only check is File.exists() with a fallback to server.log, which does not constrain traversal. The endpoint is behind admin authentication (admin console web.xml constrains /* to the admin role; REST management requires an admin token), so it is not unauthenticated. Verified that RawLogParser (not only the GlassFish-specific parsers) is selected for unrecognized content, so contents are still returned; verified that absolute-path inputs are also resolved by LogFilter.getLogFile when they exist. P1 index entries (security_call/symbol hints) were treated as navigation only and were not used as evidence; the conclusion rests on the source lines above.
candidates.impact: Disclosure of arbitrary files readable by the Payara server account (for example domain configuration containing credentials/aliases, admin key/credential stores, other applications' configuration or logs, system files such as /etc/passwd). This is a confidentiality breach that can expose administrative secrets and enable follow-on privilege escalation to the server host/domain. It is an authenticated (admin-console/REST) vulnerability, not an unauthenticated pre-auth issue.
candidates.prerequisites: A valid admin session/token for the DAS admin REST interface (or the ability to make an authenticated admin console/REST request, including via the same log-viewing UI), the logging service available (LogManager installed), and a target text file that exists and is readable by the Payara process. The attacker must supply a traversal-relative path (the code prefixes the configured logs directory when the value is non-empty). Returned content is paginated (default 40 records per call), so large files are read in repeated requests.
candidates.root_cause: The admin REST resource StructuredLogViewerResource.getRecords() binds the request query parameter `logFileName` (line 90) to a String and forwards it, via getWithType(), to LogFilter.getLogRecordsUsingQuery() (LogFilter.java lines 142-216). For the DAS branch, LogFilter builds the target path by string concatenation: `logFileDetailsForServer.substring(0, lastIndexOf(File.separator)) + File.separator + logFileName.trim()` (lines 167-168). The only guard is `new File(logFileName).exists()` (line 169); there is no normalization, no canonical-path containment check, and no whitelist of allowed log file names, so `../` sequences (or absolute-path tricks handled by getLogFile(), lines 637-652) escape the logs directory. The resolved file is then wrapped in LogFile (getLogFile -> new LogFile(fileName)) and read in LogFile.getLogEntries() (LogFile.java lines 102-155). LogParserFactory.createLogParser() selects RawLogParser for unrecognized content (LogParserFactory.java lines 102-109), and RawLogParser.parseLog() puts every line of the file into ParsedLogRecord.LOG_MESSAGE (RawLogParser.java lines 66-71), so the whole file is emitted as log records and returned to the requester in the JSON/XML LogRecordList (StructuredLogViewerResource.convertQueryResult, lines 162-198). The same concatenation flaw exists on the non-DAS/instance branch (LogFilter.java lines 394-408) and the admin console UI passes the same request-controlled value through without validation (LogViewHandlers.getLogQueryAttributes, lines 106 and 210).
candidates.title: Path traversal in admin REST log viewer allows arbitrary file read
candidates.trace: GET /management/domain/view-log/details?logFileName=<traversal> -> StructuredLogViewerResource.getRecords() (lines 87-100) -> getWithType() (lines 113-158) -> LogFilter.getLogRecordsUsingQuery(String logFileName, ...) (lines 142-216) -> path concatenation lines 167-168 and exists() line 169 -> LogFilter.getLogFile(fileName) (lines 637-652, accepts any existing path) -> LogFile.getLogEntries() (LogFile.java lines 102-155) -> LogParserFactory.createLogParser() falls back to RawLogParser (LogParserFactory.java lines 102-109) -> RawLogParser.parseLog() sets LOG_MESSAGE to each file line (lines 66-71) -> StructuredLogViewerResource.convertQueryResult() (lines 162-198) serializes the lines into the JSON/XML response. For non-DAS instances the equivalent sink is LogFilter lines 394-408.
candidates.unverified: The endpoint was not executed (no build/tests/scanners run), so runtime reachability, the exact deployed REST path, and the effect of Jersey parameter handling were not confirmed; the admin authentication requirement and token semantics were inferred from source (web.xml security-constraint, RestAdapter/SessionsResource) rather than exercised. It could not be determined from the snapshot whether an upstream fix (for example for CVE-2021-41381) was intended to cover this exact code path, or whether this snapshot corresponds to the benchmark's ground-truth CVE; the finding is submitted as a lead based on source evidence, not as a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') -> arbitrary file disclosure (CWE-200/CWE-538)

coverage_summary: Ran get_source_scope (12,030 model-visible files; binary files refused/skipped; no over-5MiB, symlink, or sensitive-name exclusions; same filters apply to B0 and P1) and get_relation_scope (index status complete: 12,030 indexed files, 110,608 symbols, 278,070 call rows, 224,269 edges, 5,025 facts; no SAST/oracle findings loaded; build/tests not run). Coverage was targeted, not exhaustive: I read and traced security-relevant Payara/GlassFish areas including the admin GUI servlets and handlers (DownloadServlet and content sources, WoodstockHandler, LogViewHandlers, AdminConsoleAuthModule, GadgetHandlers, ThemeHandlers), the admin REST service (SessionResource/SessionsResource, LogViewerResource, StructuredLogViewerResource, LogNamesResource, TemplateCommandPostResource/TemplateRestResource file uploads, Util.saveFile, CommandResourceMetaData registration), the logging backend (LogFilter, LogFilterForInstance, LogFile, LogParserFactory, RawLogParser, CollectLogFiles), EJB HTTP remoting (endpoint servlet, JAX-RS resource, initializer, admin configuration), MicroProfile JWT auth (JwtTokenParser, filters), REST monitoring auth, web-core authentication (FormAuthenticator, CsrfPreventionFilter, DefaultServlet/WebdavServlet path checks), admin backup/restore, and Payara-specific module lists. I did not read every one of the 12,030 files, and I did not inspect compiled binaries, deployment templates beyond spot checks, or the majority of locale/help/documentation resources.
limitations: No build, test execution, scanner run, or runtime probing was performed; all conclusions are static source review only.

The P1 index is syntactic/navigation-only (declarations, calls, containment, file/symbol hints) and does not prove data flow, reachability, or exploitability; index 'security_call' categories were used only as navigation hints.

Runtime reachability of the exact REST URL/method and the behavior of the Jersey/container layers (parameter decoding, authentication filter ordering, servlet mapping precedence for /ejb/* vs /*) were inferred from source and not confirmed by execution.

For the submitted candidate, the admin authentication prerequisite was inferred from web.xml security constraints and the REST session/token classes, not exercised; whether an upstream fix already targeted this code path, and whether this snapshot matches any benchmark ground truth, is unknown.

Other plausible but unverified leads (EJB invoker authorization, admin console restUrl SSRF/token leak, open redirects, EJB-over-HTTP deserialization) were not deepened to the same level as the submitted candidate; they remain unconfirmed.
The review is a single-candidate defensive assessment and is not a complete audit of the repository.

rejected_leads.lead: Deprecated EJB HTTP invoker servlet fails open on authorization (appserver/ejb/ejb-http-remoting/endpoint/src/main/java/fish/payara/ejb/invoke/InvokeEJBServlet.java lines 108-156): `if (securityEnabled) { for (role : roles) { if (!request.isUserInRole(role)) response.setStatus(403); } }` never returns/breaks, so the request is still processed and the JSON payload is used to look up and invoke EJBs; the container-applied ServletSecurity in EjbInvokerContainerInitializer (lines 77-91) and the login config in EjbInvokerService cover the JAX-RS registration (/*), not the deprecated /ejb/* servlet mapping.
rejected_leads.reason: Real-looking improper-authorization defect, but prerequisites are narrower (invoker app deployed and securityEnabled=true) and I could not fully exclude an additional container-level constraint for the legacy mapping without building/running; kept as an unconfirmed lead rather than the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Admin console DownloadServlet content sources build the upstream endpoint from the request parameter `restUrl` and attach the admin REST token (appserver/admingui/common/src/main/java/org/glassfish/admingui/common/servlet/LogViewerContentSource.java lines 82-95 and the sibling LogFiles/ClientStubs/LBConfig content sources), with RestUtil.getRequestFromServlet (RestUtil.java lines 830-838) sending a Cookie header carrying the `gfresttoken` REST token to whatever host is supplied.
rejected_leads.reason: Would allow SSRF and REST token exfiltration to an attacker host, but exploitation requires an authenticated admin to be induced to issue the request (top-level navigation/CSRF-style), and I did not verify Cookie SameSite behavior or token/cookie handling at runtime; impact chain is plausible but more conditional than the submitted path traversal.

rejected_leads.lead: Redirect-to-saved-request/path without external-URL validation: AdminConsoleAuthModule.redirectBack (appserver/admingui/common/src/main/java/org/glassfish/admingui/common/security/AdminConsoleAuthModule.java lines 368-384), RestMonitoringAuthModule (lines 161-169), and FormAuthenticator.doAuthenticate/savedRequestURL (appserver/web/web-core/src/main/java/org/apache/catalina/authenticator/FormAuthenticator.java lines 291-313, 592-603).
rejected_leads.reason: Open-redirect class issue only (lower impact), and web-naming org.apache.naming.Util.normalize collapses '//' and backslashes for request paths while the exact unnormalized value returned by getRequestURI() at the redirect point was not verified; not enough evidence for the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Untrusted Java deserialization in the EJB-over-HTTP JAX-RS endpoint (ObjectStreamMessageBodyReader / ObjectStreamInvokeMethodMessageBodyReader in appserver/ejb/ejb-http-remoting/endpoint, plus the deprecated servlet's Class.forName on request-supplied class names).
rejected_leads.reason: Deserialization is part of the documented wire protocol and the endpoint is disabled by default; without a gadget-chain analysis or proof that security-disabled deployment is a supported non-default state, this is a hardening concern rather than a demonstrated vulnerability.

summary: The strongest source-evidenced issue in this Payara 5.2022.4-SNAPSHOT tree is a path traversal / arbitrary file read in the admin REST log viewer: the caller-supplied `logFileName` query parameter of `/management/domain/view-log/details` is concatenated verbatim into a filesystem path by LogFilter and then opened and line-parsed, with no canonicalization or containment check. Because the parser chosen for unknown formats (RawLogParser) emits every line as a log record, the file content is returned to the caller as JSON. The defect is Payara-specific in the sense that the admin REST/admin console log-viewing stack is exposed by this distribution, and it matches the well-known Payara "path traversal in the admin console log viewer" vulnerability class. Two other security-relevant defects were identified but not submitted: a fail-open authorization check in the deprecated EJB HTTP invoker servlet, and unvalidated `restUrl` SSRF/REST-token disclosure in the admin console download content sources.
